extracted.intended_audience: students preparing for mathematical olympiads / contest problem solvers in graph theory
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture-style notes introducing basic graph theory definitions, standard theorems, proof techniques, and sample Olympiad problems with hints; aimed to train problem-solving in graph-theoretic Olympiad questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a graph
rubrics_metrics.description: A graph G = (V, E) is a collection V of vertices and E ⊂ V × V of edges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark that graphs are typically represented by drawings connecting endpoints with curves; this is the foundational object for all subsequent statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple graph (implicit requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If every edge links a unique pair of distinct vertices, then the graph is simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most work in these notes is with simple graphs; multiple edges and loops are typically not considered unless stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjacency
rubrics_metrics.description: Two vertices are adjacent if there is an edge that has them as endpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic vocabulary used throughout; adjacency underlies definitions of paths, cycles, degree, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bipartite graph
rubrics_metrics.description: A graph is bipartite if the vertex set can be partitioned into two sets V1 ∪ V2 such that edges only run between V1 and V2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful characterization: a graph is bipartite iff it has no odd cycles. For proofs, color by parity of distances from a chosen vertex per connected component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chromatic number
rubrics_metrics.description: The chromatic number of a graph is the minimum number of colors needed to color vertices so adjacent vertices receive different colors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An upper bound: chromatic number ≤ maximum degree + 1 via a greedy coloring algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clique / Complete graph
rubrics_metrics.description: A clique on n vertices, denoted Kn, is the n-vertex graph with all (n choose 2) possible edges (complete graph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kn and complete multipartite variants (e.g., Turán graphs) are central extremal examples in many problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connected graph
rubrics_metrics.description: A graph is connected if there is a path between every pair of distinct vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connected components partition the vertex set into induced subgraphs that are connected and pairwise nonadjacent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Path / Walk / Cycle distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: A walk is a sequence of not-necessarily-distinct, pairwise-adjacent vertices. A path is a sequence of distinct, pairwise-adjacent vertices. A cycle is a path whose first and last vertices are adjacent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use walks when edges/vertices may repeat; use paths for simple connectivity arguments and cycles for parity/planarity arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree and incident edge
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree d(v) of a vertex v is the number of edges incident to v. An edge e is incident to vertex v if v is an endpoint of e.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Degree-sum and parity arguments are fundamental (see sum of degrees = 2E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eulerian circuit
rubrics_metrics.description: An Eulerian circuit is a walk that traverses every edge exactly once and returns to its starting point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A connected graph with all vertex degrees even has an Eulerian circuit. Construction: start a nonrepeating-edge walk; splice cycles when unused edges touch the current walk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forest and tree
rubrics_metrics.description: A forest is a graph with no cycles (not necessarily connected). A tree is a connected graph with no cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trees have multiple equivalent characterizations: every tree has a leaf (degree 1); every connected graph that is a tree has exactly V−1 edges; every tree can be constructed by starting with a vertex and adding leaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induced subgraph
rubrics_metrics.description: If U is a subset of vertices, the induced subgraph G[U] is obtained by deleting all vertices outside U and keeping only edges with both endpoints in U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induced subgraphs are used for component/partition arguments and minor/embedding constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamiltonian path / cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hamiltonian path includes every vertex; a Hamiltonian cycle is a cycle that includes every vertex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamiltonicity is a global property often addressed by sufficient conditions or constructive methods; not central in these basic lemmas but defined for use in problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of degrees equals twice edges
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of all vertex degrees equals twice the number of edges (∑ d(v) = 2E). Deduce that the number of odd-degree vertices is even.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by double-counting incident (vertex,edge) pairs. This parity consequence is routinely used in Olympiad problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every tree has a leaf (degree 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tree contains a vertex of degree exactly 1 (called a leaf).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: if all degrees ≥ 2, a non-backtracking walk must eventually repeat a vertex, yielding a cycle, contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing and deconstructing trees by leaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tree can be constructed by starting with a single vertex and adding one new leaf at a time (equivalently, every tree can be destructed by removing a leaf repeatedly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for inductive proofs on trees and counting arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every connected graph contains a spanning tree
rubrics_metrics.description: A connected graph contains a spanning tree, a subgraph that is a tree including all original vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct by repeatedly deleting edges from cycles (or see BFS/DFS to build a spanning tree). Useful to reduce general connected graphs to trees for some arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tree iff has V − 1 edges (connected)
rubrics_metrics.description: A connected graph is a tree if and only if it has exactly V − 1 edges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward: trees constructed by adding one leaf add one edge per new vertex. Reverse: use existence of spanning tree and count edges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connected components partition
rubrics_metrics.description: Vertices can be partitioned into sets V1 ∪ ... ∪ Vr where each induced subgraph G[Vi] is connected and there are no edges between distinct Vi, Vj (the connected components).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trivial but frequently invoked; handle each connected component separately for coloring, parity, or traversal arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of bipartite graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: A graph is bipartite if and only if it has no odd cycles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color vertices by parity of distance from a chosen root in each component; conversely, any odd cycle prevents a 2-coloring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eulerian circuit existence condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Every connected graph with all vertex degrees even has an Eulerian circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct by starting a maximal nonrepeating-edge walk (gives a cycle); if unused edges remain, find vertex on current walk adjacent to unused edge and splice another cycle; repeat until all edges used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greedy coloring bound
rubrics_metrics.description: The chromatic number of a graph is always ≤ its maximum degree plus one (χ ≤ Δ+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by ordering vertices arbitrarily and assigning to each vertex the smallest available color not used by its already-colored neighbors (greedy algorithm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting / extremal technique (double-counting and convexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use counting in two ways and convexity/inequalities to bound numbers of substructures forced by edge counts (e.g., lower bounds on numbers of K1,r stars in a graph with m edges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ∑ d_i = 2m; apply convexity/inequalities such as Jensen/Power-mean variants to lower/upper bound combinatorial counts; these are the basis of extremal graph arguments like Turán's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turán graph and Turán's theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Let Tr(n) be the complete r-partite graph with n vertices distributed among r parts as evenly as possible. For r ≥ 3, the Turán graph Tr−1(n) is the unique n-vertex graph with the maximum number of edges subject to having no Kr subgraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turan graphs are extremal; use part-size convexity arguments to show any graph avoiding Kr has at most as many edges as the corresponding Turán graph. Useful for triangle-free and general Kr-free extremal problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extremal-subgraph forcing (stars and copies count)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any integer r ≥ 2, an n-vertex graph with m edges must have at least n·( (2m/n) choose r ) subgraphs isomorphic to the r-pointed star K1,r (and related lower bounds for K1,2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by letting d_i be degrees and applying convexity inequalities on degree sequences; useful to force small substructures when edge density is known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique: consider longest path
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove existence of long paths/cycles, take a longest path and analyze degrees/neighbor constraints of its endpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show a graph with minimum degree δ ≥ 2 contains a cycle of size ≥ δ+1 by analyzing neighbors of an endpoint of a longest path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Max-cut and partitioning technique
rubrics_metrics.description: For partitioning problems where each vertex wants many neighbors across the cut, take a max-cut (a bipartition maximizing crossing edges) to guarantee properties like each vertex having at least half its neighbors across the cut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to ensure balance properties and to construct colorings/partitions with component-size constraints (e.g., relaxed colorings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hall's Marriage Theorem (perfect matching criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: For bipartite G = (A ∪ B, E), A has a perfect matching to B iff for every S ⊂ A, |N(S)| ≥ |S|, where N(S) is the neighbor set in B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canonical tool for existence of matchings; used also to decompose nonnegative-integer matrices into permutation matrices and in combinatorial design constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable Marriage Theorem (existence of stable matching)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any bipartite graph and any collection of preference orderings for vertices, a stable matching always exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gale–Shapley algorithm provides a constructive proof; concept used to reason about stability vs cardinality tradeoffs in matchings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique: iterative deletion of low-degree vertices
rubrics_metrics.description: To find a subgraph with high minimum degree, repeatedly delete vertices of degree below a threshold until the remaining graph has the desired minimum degree (or stops when small).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: from average degree d, delete vertices of degree < d/2 to produce a subgraph with minimum degree ≥ d/2; used to embed trees and other substructures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ramsey number definition and basic inductive bound
rubrics_metrics.description: R(s,t) is the minimal n such that every red-blue coloring of edges of Kn contains either a red Ks or blue Kt. Basic bound: R(s,t) ≤ R(s−1,t) + R(s,t−1) (hence binomial upper bounds by induction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vertex-neighborhood partitioning by color into red-neighbors and blue-neighbors to apply the inductive step. Apply recursively for multi-color extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planarity: Euler formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Every connected planar graph satisfies V − E + F = 2, where F is number of faces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Euler formula with face-perimeter double-counting (∑ face perimeters = 2E) to derive planar inequalities such as E ≤ 3V − 6 for simple planar graphs; key to proving nonplanarity of K5 and K3,3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planarity: face perimeter and E ≤ 3V − 6 bound
rubrics_metrics.description: In a connected, planar, simple graph, E ≤ 3V − 6 because every face has perimeter ≥ 3 and 2E ≥ 3F, combined with Euler formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger bounds exist when triangles are forbidden (e.g., for bipartite planar graphs use 2E ≥ 4F), enabling quick proofs K3,3 and K5 are nonplanar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-color theorem (statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every planar graph is 4-colorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a famous result (not proved here); used as a high-level fact about planar graph coloring constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-solving mindset: reduce to extremal configurations
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked for minimal or maximal edge counts guaranteeing a property, consider extremal (maximal disconnected / minimal connected) configurations, convexity, or partition into cliques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: to find minimal N guaranteeing connectivity, consider maximal disconnected graphs (components must be cliques) and apply convexity to show extremum occurs with one large clique and isolated vertices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix decomposition via Hall's theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: An n×n nonnegative integer matrix with each row and column summing to m can be written as a sum of m permutation matrices, via Hall's theorem applied to a bipartite multigraph representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct bipartite graph with multiplicities equal to entries; apply Hall to extract permutation matrices inductively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique: splicing cycles / walk splicing
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing Eulerian circuits or combining partial traversals, splice cycles/walks together at common vertices to form longer circuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in Eulerian construction: obtain a cycle, then find unused edges incident to cycle vertices and splice another cycle at that vertex; repeat.
